source_text: His igitur tot ac tantis testibus conprobatur unius dei potestate ac prouidentia mundum gubernari, cuius uim maiestatemque tantam esse dicit in Timaeo Plato, ut eam neque mente concipere neque uerbis enarrare quisquam possit ob) nimiam et inaestimabilem potestatem. dubitet uero aliquis an quicquam difficile aut inpossibile sit deo, qui tanta tamque mirifica opera prouidentia excogitauit, uirtute constituit, ratione perfecit, nunc autem spiritu sustentet, potestate moderetur, inexcogitabilis ineffabilis et nulli alii satis notus quam sibi? unde mihi de tanta maiestate saepius cogitanti qui deos colunt interdum uideri solent tam caeci, tam incogitabiles, tam excordes, tam non multum a mutis animalibus differentes, qui credant eos qui geniti sint maris ac feminae coitu aliquid maiestatis diuinaeque uirtutis habere potuisse, cum Sibylla Erythraea dicat: ou οὐ δύνατ\' ἀνδρὸς ἑϰ μηρῶν μήτρας τε θεὸς τετυπωμένος εἶναι. quod si est uerum, sicuti est, apparet Herculem Apollinem Liberum Mercurium Iouemque ipsum cum ceteris homines fuisse, quoniam sunt ex duobus sexibus nati. quid est autem a deo tam remotum quam id opus, quod ipse ad propagandam subolem mortalibus tribuit et quod sine substantia corporali nullum potest esse? dii ergo si sunt inmortales et aeterni, quid opus est altero sexu — nimirum ut generent? ipsa progenie quid opus est, cum successione non egeant qui semper sunt futuri? nam profecto in hominibus ceterisque animantibus diuersitas sexus et coitio et generatio nullam habet aliam rationem nisi ut omnia genera uiuentium, quoniam sunt condicione mortalitatis obitura, mutua possint successione seruari, deo autem, qui est sempiternus, neque alter sexus neque successio necessaria est. dicet aliquis ut habeat uel ministros uel in quos possit ipse dominari.\' quid igitur sexu opus est feminino, cum deus, qui est omnipotens ut uocatur, sine usu et opera feminae possit. filios procreare? nam si quibusdam minutis animalibus id praestitit, ut sibi e foliis natos et suauibus herbis ore legant, cur existimet aliquis ipsum deum nisi ex permixtione sexus alterius non posse generare? illos igitur quos inperiti et insipientes tamquam deos et nuncupant et adorant, nemo est tam inconsideratus quin intellegat fuisse mortales. \'quomodo ergo\' inquiet aliquis \'dii crediti sunt?\' nimirum quia reges maximi ac potentissimi fuerunt, ob merita uirtutum suarum aut munerum aut artium repertarum, cum cari fuissent iis quibus inperitauerant, in memoriam sunt consecrati. quod si quis dubitat, res eorum gestas et facta consideret, quae uniuersa tam poetae quam historici ueteres prodiderunt.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore by these so many and so great witnesses it is confirmed that the world is governed by the power and providence of one God, whose power and majesty are so great, as Plato says in Timaeus, that no one can conceive it with the mind or express it with words because of the excessive and immeasurable power. But let someone doubt whether anything is difficult or impossible for God, who with providence devised, with virtue established, with reason perfected, and now sustains with spirit, and moderates with power, such great and wondrous works, incomprehensible, ineffable, and known to no one sufficiently except to himself? Whence to me, thinking often about such great majesty, those who worship gods sometimes seem so blind, so unknowing, so foolish, differing not much from mute animals, who believe that those born from the union of male and female can have some divine majesty and virtue, when the Erythraean Sibyl says: for it is not possible for a god to be formed from the thighs and womb of a man. Which if it is true, as it is, it appears that Hercules, Apollo, Liber, Mercury, and Jupiter himself, along with the others, were men, since they were born from two sexes. What is further from God than that work, which he himself gave to mortals for propagating offspring, and which cannot exist without bodily substance? Therefore, if the gods are immortal and eternal, what need is there for another sex - namely, to generate? What need is there for progeny, since they do not need succession, as they will always be? For certainly, in humans and other animals, the diversity of sex and coition and generation have no other reason than that all kinds of living things, since they are mortal, can be preserved by mutual succession, but for God, who is eternal, neither another sex nor succession is necessary. Someone will say, so that he may have either ministers or those over whom he can dominate. What need, therefore, is there for the female sex, since God, who is omnipotent, as he is called, can procreate sons without the use and work of a female? For if he granted this to certain small animals, so that they are born from leaves and sweet herbs and gather them with their mouth, why would someone think that God himself cannot generate except from the mixture of another sex? Therefore, no one is so inconsiderate as not to understand that those whom the unskilled and foolish call and worship as gods were mortals. How, therefore, were they believed to be gods? Namely, because they were the greatest and most powerful kings, consecrated to memory because of the merits of their virtues or gifts or discovered arts, when they were dear to those whom they ruled. But if someone doubts, let him consider their deeds and actions, which both the old poets and historians have handed down.

pass_b_english: By such a multitude and magnitude of witnesses, it is confirmed that the world is governed by the power and providence of one God. Plato declares in the Timaeus that his power and majesty are so great that no one can conceive them with the mind or express them in words, because of their excessive and immeasurable power. But let someone doubt whether anything is difficult or impossible for God, who by providence devised, by virtue established, by reason perfected, and now by spirit sustains and by power moderates such great and wondrous works — incomprehensible, ineffable, and known to no one sufficiently except to himself? When I reflect often on such majesty, those who worship gods sometimes seem so blind, so unknowing, so foolish, differing little from mute animals. They believe that beings born from the union of male and female can possess some divine majesty and virtue, even though the Erythraean Sibyl says: it is not possible for a god to be formed from the thighs and womb of a man. If that is true, as it is, it appears that Hercules, Apollo, Liber, Mercury, and Jupiter himself, along with the others, were men, since they were born from two sexes. What is more remote from God than that act which he himself gave to mortals for propagating offspring, an act that cannot exist without bodily substance? Therefore, if the gods are immortal and eternal, what need is there for another sex — namely, to generate? What need is there for progeny, since they do not need succession, being always future? For certainly in humans and other animals, the diversity of sex, coition, and generation has no other reason than that all kinds of living things, because they are subject to mortality, may be preserved by mutual succession; but for God, who is eternal, neither another sex nor succession is necessary. Someone will say: so that he may have either ministers or those over whom he can dominate. What need, then, is there for the female sex, since God, who is omnipotent as he is called, can procreate sons without the use and work of a female? For if he granted this to certain small animals, so that they are born from leaves and sweet herbs and gather them with their mouth, why would anyone think that God himself cannot generate except from the mixture of another sex? Therefore, no one is so inconsiderate as not to understand that those whom the unskilled and foolish call and worship as gods were mortals. How, then, were they believed to be gods? Namely, because they were the greatest and most powerful kings, consecrated to memory on account of the merits of their virtues or gifts or discovered arts, when they were dear to those whom they ruled. If anyone doubts, let him consider their deeds and actions, which both the ancient poets and historians have handed down.
